title: Continuum field theory of matchgate tensor network ensembles
comment: 42 pages total (27 main text, 15 appendix), 8 figures
summary: Tensor networks provide discrete representations of quantum many-body systems, yet their precise connection to continuum field theories remains relatively poorly understood. Invoking a notion of typicality, we develop a continuum description for random ensembles of two-dimensional fermionic matchgate tensor networks with spatially fluctuating parameters. As a diagnostic of the resulting universal physics, we analyze disorder-averaged moments of fermionic two-point functions, both in flat geometry and on a hyperbolic disk, where curvature reshapes their long-distance structure. We show that disorder drives universal long-distance behavior governed by a nonlinear sigma-model of symmetry class D with a topological term, placing random matchgate networks in direct correspondence with the thermal quantum Hall problem. The resulting phase structure includes localized phases, quantum Hall criticality, and a robust thermal metal with diffusive correlations and spontaneous replica-symmetry breaking. Weak non-Gaussian deformations reduce the symmetry to discrete permutations, generate a mass for the Goldstone modes, and suppress long-range correlations. In this way, typicality offers a route from ensembles of discrete tensor networks to continuum quantum field theories.

AI.tldr: Random 2D fermionic matchgate tensor networks exhibit universal continuum physics described by a class D nonlinear sigma model with topological term, connecting to thermal quantum Hall physics with localized, critical, and thermal metal phases.
AI.motivation: To establish a precise connection between discrete tensor network representations of quantum many-body systems and continuum field theories, particularly for random ensembles of fermionic matchgate tensor networks with spatial parameter fluctuations.
AI.method: Using typicality to develop continuum descriptions for random ensembles of 2D fermionic matchgate tensor networks; analyzing disorder-averaged moments of fermionic two-point functions in both flat and hyperbolic geometries; studying the universal long-distance behavior driven by disorder.
AI.result: Disorder drives universal long-distance behavior governed by a nonlinear sigma-model of symmetry class D with topological term, establishing direct correspondence with thermal quantum Hall problem; phase structure includes localized phases, quantum Hall criticality, and robust thermal metal with diffusive correlations and spontaneous replica-symmetry breaking; weak non-Gaussian deformations reduce symmetry to discrete permutations, generate Goldstone mode mass, and suppress long-range correlations.
AI.conclusion: Typicality provides a systematic route from ensembles of discrete tensor networks to continuum quantum field theories, establishing random matchgate networks as a bridge between discrete tensor network representations and continuum field theory descriptions of quantum many-body systems.

title: Optimal recovery for quantum error correction
summary: The calculation of the error threshold of quantum error correcting codes typically proceeds as follows. First, syndromes are measured. Then, a decoder infers the error chain and the corresponding correction is applied. The threshold is then defined as the largest correctable error rate, with the maximum-likelihood decoder corresponding to the ``optimal'' threshold. However, a broader set of operations could be used to recover quantum information. The true optimal threshold should be optimised over all possible recovery schemes, which can be described by quantum channels. Here, we study such optimal recovery channels and their thresholds $p_\mathrm{th}^\mathrm{opt}$. We introduce an information-theoretic quantity, mutual trace distance, which provides a necessary and sufficient diagnostic for sharply determining $p_\mathrm{th}^\mathrm{opt}$ without explicit optimisation. In contrast, previous works give a lower bound on $p_\mathrm{th}^\mathrm{opt}$ by specifying particular recovery schemes, e.g. Schumacher-Westmoreland (SW) which provides coherent information as a diagnostic to lower bound $p^\mathrm{opt}_\mathrm{th}$. We prove that the Petz and SW recovery schemes are optimal, i.e. their threshold is $p_\mathrm{th}^\mathrm{opt}$. With their optimality established, we explore the structure of optimal and non-optimal recovery schemes and their phase diagrams.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces mutual trace distance as an information-theoretic diagnostic for determining the optimal error threshold of quantum error correcting codes over all possible recovery schemes, proving that Petz and Schumacher-Westmoreland recovery schemes achieve this optimal threshold.
AI.motivation: Traditional quantum error correction threshold calculations rely on syndrome measurement and decoding, but the true optimal threshold should be optimized over all possible recovery schemes described by quantum channels, not just maximum-likelihood decoding.
AI.method: Introduces mutual trace distance as an information-theoretic quantity that provides necessary and sufficient conditions for determining the optimal threshold without explicit optimization, and analyzes Petz and Schumacher-Westmoreland recovery schemes.
AI.result: Proves that Petz and Schumacher-Westmoreland recovery schemes are optimal, achieving the true optimal threshold p_th^opt, and explores the structure of optimal vs non-optimal recovery schemes and their phase diagrams.
AI.conclusion: Mutual trace distance provides a sharp diagnostic for optimal error thresholds, and established recovery schemes (Petz and SW) achieve optimal performance, enabling better understanding of recovery scheme structure and phase transitions in quantum error correction.

title: In-situ Characterization of Light-Matter Coupling in Multimode Circuit-QED Systems
summary: Multimode cavity-QED systems can be leveraged to explore a wide range of physical phenomena; however, a complex multimode environment makes systematic characterization of light-matter interactions challenging. Here we present a general measurement protocol, applicable to both atomic and synthetic cavity-QED systems, that enables the determination of coupling to individual photonic modes. The method leverages measurements of the AC-Stark and Kerr effects, along with known detuning dependencies, to eliminate the need for single-photon resolution, independent photon-number calibration, or insertion-loss calibration. We demonstrate the method using a superconducting transmon qubit coupled to a one-dimensional microwave resonator lattice. We validate the consistency of the extracted light-matter couplings $g$ determined at multiple qubit detunings, and from the self-Kerr and cross-Kerr shifts for three photon modes, which provide separate measurements of $g$ for each of the three modes.

AI.tldr: A measurement protocol for determining light-matter coupling strengths in multimode cavity-QED systems without requiring single-photon resolution or calibration of photon numbers and insertion losses.
AI.motivation: Multimode cavity-QED systems enable exploration of diverse physical phenomena, but their complex multimode environments make systematic characterization of light-matter interactions challenging. Existing methods often require demanding experimental capabilities like single-photon resolution and precise calibration.
AI.method: A general measurement protocol leveraging AC-Stark and Kerr effects with known detuning dependencies. The method uses measurements of self-Kerr and cross-Kerr shifts at multiple qubit detunings to extract coupling strengths g for individual photonic modes without needing single-photon resolution, independent photon-number calibration, or insertion-loss calibration.
AI.result: The method was demonstrated using a superconducting transmon qubit coupled to a 1D microwave resonator lattice. Consistent coupling strengths g were extracted at multiple qubit detunings from both self-Kerr and cross-Kerr shifts for three photon modes, providing separate measurements of g for each mode.
AI.conclusion: The presented protocol provides a general, calibration-free approach for characterizing light-matter interactions in multimode cavity-QED systems, validated through experimental demonstration with superconducting circuits.

title: Two-dimensional matter-wave interferometer, rotational dynamics, and spin contrast
summary: We investigate a two-dimensional matter-wave interferometer where both spatial and rotational dynamics of a nanoparticle are intertwined in closing the one-loop interferometer in the Stern-Gerlach type setup. We consider the spin-contrast of the nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centred nanodiamond in combination with a two-dimensional magnetic field setup to extend the one-dimensional Stern--Gerlach interferometry. We analyse the dynamical motion along with the rigid rotation under the influence of the external magnetic field. Regarding rotation, we incorporate Euler-angle dynamics to analyse the stability of rotational degrees of freedom and their influence on the spin contrast to address the Humpty-Dumpty problem. We show that by imparting external rotation provides the gyroscopic stability to the liberating mode of the NV-spin and hence helps to improve the contrast. Our scheme creates a tiny spatial superposition of size $\sim 0.21~{\rm μm}$ for mass $m=10^{-17}$kg in less than $t\sim 0.013$s.

AI.tldr: Two-dimensional matter-wave interferometer using NV-center nanodiamond with Stern-Gerlach setup achieves 0.21 μm spatial superposition for 10⁻¹⁷ kg mass in 0.013 s, with rotational stability improving spin contrast.
AI.motivation: Extend one-dimensional Stern-Gerlach interferometry to two dimensions by incorporating both spatial and rotational dynamics, addressing the Humpty-Dumpty problem (reversibility of quantum superposition) through gyroscopic stabilization of rotational degrees of freedom.
AI.method: Use spin-contrast of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in nanodiamond combined with two-dimensional magnetic field setup; analyze dynamical motion and rigid rotation under external magnetic field; incorporate Euler-angle dynamics to study rotational stability and its effect on spin contrast; impart external rotation for gyroscopic stabilization.
AI.result: External rotation provides gyroscopic stability to liberating mode of NV-spin, improving contrast; creates spatial superposition of size ∼0.21 μm for mass m=10⁻¹⁷ kg in less than t∼0.013 s.
AI.conclusion: Two-dimensional Stern-Gerlach interferometer with rotational stabilization successfully addresses Humpty-Dumpty problem and enables creation of macroscopic spatial superpositions on micrometer scale with improved spin contrast.

title: Identification of the I$_{10}$ Donor in ZnO as a Sn--Li Complex with Large Hyperfine Interaction
summary: Donor impurities in wide direct band gap semiconductors provide a promising platform for spin--photon quantum technologies by combining a donor spin qubit with optically addressable transitions. In ZnO, the shallow donor with the largest reported binding energy has long been associated with the I$_{10}$ bound exciton line, but its microscopic origin has remained unresolved. Here we demonstrate the controlled formation and identification of this donor as a Sn--Li complex through a combination of ion implantation, annealing, optical spectroscopy, and first-principles calculations. Resonant two-laser coherent population trapping measurements reveal an electron--$^{119}$Sn hyperfine interaction of $392 \pm 15$\,MHz, establishing a coupled electron--spin--1/2, nuclear--spin--1/2 system with one of the largest hyperfine couplings reported for shallow donors in semiconductors. Density functional theory calculations show that a nearest-neighbor Sn$_{\mathrm{Zn}}$--Li$_{\mathrm{Zn}}$ complex has favorable formation energetics, donor character with the electron localized on Sn, and an extrapolated hyperfine interaction consistent with experiment. The large donor binding energy and excited-state structure indicate enhanced thermal robustness of the optical transition relative to conventional group--III donors, while the strong hyperfine interaction enables fast electron--nuclear spin control and prospects for direct nuclear--spin--photon interfaces. We further observe efficient optically induced nuclear spin polarization, highlighting a path toward nuclear spin initialization. More broadly, our results reveal how a donor--acceptor complex can access previously unexplored regimes of shallow donor physics, extending the design space of quantum defects beyond isolated substitutional dopants.

AI.tldr: Researchers identify the Sn-Li complex as the origin of the I10 bound exciton line in ZnO, demonstrating controlled formation via ion implantation and revealing exceptionally strong electron-nuclear hyperfine coupling for quantum applications.
AI.motivation: The microscopic origin of the I10 bound exciton line in ZnO has remained unresolved despite its importance as the shallow donor with the largest reported binding energy, which makes it promising for spin-photon quantum technologies.
AI.method: Combination of ion implantation, annealing, optical spectroscopy, resonant two-laser coherent population trapping measurements, and first-principles density functional theory calculations to identify and characterize the donor complex.
AI.result: Identification of the donor as a Sn-Li complex with electron-119Sn hyperfine interaction of 392 ± 15 MHz, one of the largest reported for shallow donors. DFT calculations confirm favorable formation energetics, donor character with electron localized on Sn, and hyperfine interaction consistent with experiment.
AI.conclusion: The Sn-Li complex represents a new class of quantum defects with enhanced thermal robustness, strong hyperfine interaction enabling fast spin control, and prospects for nuclear-spin-photon interfaces, extending the design space beyond isolated substitutional dopants.

title: Classical Explanations in (and of) General Probabilistic Theories
summary: We introduce a notion of the ``explanation" of one (generalized) probabilistic model by another as particular kind of span in the category $\Prob$ of probabilistic models and morphisms. We show that explanations compose under a standard pullback construction (notwithstanding that $\Prob$ does not support arbitrary pullbacks). We then show that every locally-finite probabilistic model has a canonical, sharp classical explanation. The construction is functorial, so every locally-finite probabilistic theory has a canonical, sharp classical (though of course, usually non-local) representation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a formal notion of "explanation" between probabilistic models as spans in the category Prob, shows these compose via pullbacks, and proves every locally-finite probabilistic model has a canonical sharp classical explanation.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous categorical framework for understanding how one probabilistic model can explain another, addressing the need for formal definitions of explanation in probabilistic reasoning and establishing connections between generalized probabilistic models and classical representations.
AI.method: Define explanation as a particular kind of span in the category Prob of probabilistic models and morphisms. Show explanations compose under pullback construction despite Prob lacking arbitrary pullbacks. Prove every locally-finite probabilistic model has a canonical sharp classical explanation via functorial construction.
AI.result: 1) Explanations compose via standard pullback construction in Prob. 2) Every locally-finite probabilistic model has a canonical sharp classical explanation. 3) The construction is functorial, giving every locally-finite probabilistic theory a canonical sharp classical (though typically non-local) representation.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a categorical foundation for explanations in probabilistic modeling, demonstrating that explanations compose naturally and that all locally-finite probabilistic models can be explained by sharp classical models, providing a bridge between generalized and classical probability theories.

title: Quantum Wavemetry via the Mth-Power Unitary of a Mach-Zehnder Interferometer
summary: A quantum wavemetry scheme based on the coherence de Broglie wavelength (CBW) is proposed using an M coupled Mach Zehnder interferometer (MZI) architecture to achieve superresolution sensing and metrology. Although CBW does not attain the Heisenberg limit, it circumvents the key practical limitations of N00N state based quantum sensing, including restricted photon number N, reduced fringe visibility, and strong susceptibility to photon loss. The CBW approach enables loss tolerant operation with arbitrarily large M, while maintaining near unity fringe visibility. Fully compatible with coherence optics, the CBW scheme can be directly integrated into conventional wavemetry systems, providing both superresolution and enhanced sensitivity. A proof of principle experiment demonstrating CBW based superresolution is implemented using a Sagnac integrated round trip MZI structure for M=2, validating the feasibility of the proposed quantum wavemetry design.

AI.tldr: Quantum wavemetry scheme using coherence de Broglie wavelength (CBW) with M coupled Mach-Zehnder interferometers achieves superresolution sensing while overcoming practical limitations of N00N state quantum sensing.
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum sensing approach that achieves superresolution while circumventing the practical limitations of N00N state-based quantum sensing, including restricted photon number, reduced fringe visibility, and strong susceptibility to photon loss.
AI.method: Proposes a quantum wavemetry scheme based on coherence de Broglie wavelength (CBW) using an M coupled Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) architecture. The approach leverages coherence optics and can be integrated into conventional wavemetry systems.
AI.result: The CBW approach enables loss-tolerant operation with arbitrarily large M while maintaining near-unity fringe visibility. A proof-of-principle experiment using a Sagnac integrated round-trip MZI structure for M=2 successfully demonstrates CBW-based superresolution.
AI.conclusion: The CBW-based quantum wavemetry scheme provides both superresolution and enhanced sensitivity, is fully compatible with coherence optics, and can be directly integrated into conventional wavemetry systems, offering a practical alternative to N00N state-based quantum sensing.

title: Localization Without Disorder: Quantum Walks on Structured Graphs
summary: Continuous-time quantum walks (CTQWs) exhibit localization phenomena that differ fundamentally from their classical counterparts, yet the precise relationship between network structure, spectral degeneracy, and confined dynamics remains incompletely understood. In this work, we present a complete analytical characterization of localization in CTQWs on two highly symmetric graph families: barbell graphs and star-of-cliques graphs. These networks combine pronounced spectral degeneracy with modular structure, enabling exact diagonalization and explicit computation of both eigenstate and dynamical inverse participation ratios (IPRs). Our analysis reveals that localization is governed by the interplay between degenerate subspaces, which generate families of confined modes, and hybridization between invariant subspaces, which redistributes spectral weight. Notably, the dynamical IPR can exceed expectations based solely on eigenstate IPRs, demonstrating that coherent superposition within degenerate eigenspaces enhances confinement. By connecting IPR values to the effective number of vertices visited, we provide a structural diagnostic for predicting quantum transport outcomes in modular networks, establishing that connectivity alone can determine where and how strongly a quantum walk localizes.

AI.tldr: Complete analytical characterization of localization in continuous-time quantum walks on barbell and star-of-cliques graphs reveals that spectral degeneracy and modular structure govern confinement, with coherent superposition in degenerate eigenspaces enhancing localization beyond eigenstate expectations.
AI.motivation: The relationship between network structure, spectral degeneracy, and confined dynamics in continuous-time quantum walks remains incompletely understood, despite fundamental differences from classical localization phenomena.
AI.method: Analytical characterization of localization in CTQWs on two highly symmetric graph families (barbell graphs and star-of-cliques graphs) using exact diagonalization and explicit computation of both eigenstate and dynamical inverse participation ratios (IPRs).
AI.result: Localization is governed by interplay between degenerate subspaces (generating confined modes) and hybridization between invariant subspaces (redistributing spectral weight). Dynamical IPR can exceed expectations based solely on eigenstate IPRs, demonstrating that coherent superposition within degenerate eigenspaces enhances confinement.
AI.conclusion: By connecting IPR values to effective number of vertices visited, the work provides a structural diagnostic for predicting quantum transport outcomes in modular networks, establishing that connectivity alone can determine where and how strongly a quantum walk localizes.

title: Ramsey correlation spectroscopy with phase cycling using a single quantum sensor
summary: Magnetic spectroscopy at the nanoscale provides unique insights into material properties and dynamics, with quantum sensors like nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers being ideally suited for these scales. However, detecting low-frequency signals remains a challenge due to finite coherence times ($T_2^*$), as signals oscillating slower than $1/T_2^*$ decay before sufficient phase accumulation occurs. We present RESOLUTE (Ramsey corrElation SpectroscOpy puLse seqUence wiTh phasE cycling), a protocol that overcomes these limitations by combining Ramsey measurements with correlation spectroscopy. By storing accumulated phase as a population imbalance during a correlation period ($T_\mathrm{corr} < T_1$) between two sensing periods, RESOLUTE generates an effective coherence time $T_2^p > T_2^*$. This shifts the frequency-matching condition to the correlation time, enabling detection in the previously inaccessible spectral region between $1/T_1$ and $1/T_2^p$. We experimentally demonstrate an extension of the effective coherence time from $T_2^* = 0.38\,μs$ to $T_2^p = 5.1\,μs$, surpassing Hahn Echo measurements. The technique successfully detects $^{13}$C nuclear spin Larmor precession at fields as low as 49$\,$G ($\sim$50$\,$kHz). We further provide theoretical insight using Fisher information to characterize RESOLUTE's frequency estimation capabilities compared to existing protocols. Finally, by integrating adiabatic pulses and phase cycling, we demonstrate robust spin control and effective DC signal extraction. These advancements provide enhanced sensitivity to weak dipolar interactions, essential for single-molecule imaging and quantum sensing applications.

AI.tldr: RESOLUTE protocol extends NV center coherence time via correlation spectroscopy, enabling detection of low-frequency magnetic signals previously inaccessible due to finite T₂* limitations.
AI.motivation: Overcome the challenge of detecting low-frequency magnetic signals with NV centers, where signals oscillating slower than 1/T₂* decay before sufficient phase accumulation occurs, limiting nanoscale magnetic spectroscopy applications.
AI.method: Combines Ramsey measurements with correlation spectroscopy by storing accumulated phase as population imbalance during correlation period (T_corr < T₁) between two sensing periods, generating effective coherence time T₂^p > T₂*.
AI.result: Experimentally extended effective coherence time from T₂* = 0.38 μs to T₂^p = 5.1 μs (surpassing Hahn Echo), detected ¹³C nuclear spin Larmor precession at fields as low as 49 G (~50 kHz), and demonstrated robust spin control with DC signal extraction.
AI.conclusion: RESOLUTE enables detection in previously inaccessible spectral region between 1/T₁ and 1/T₂^p, providing enhanced sensitivity to weak dipolar interactions essential for single-molecule imaging and quantum sensing applications.

title: Classical Simulability from Operator Entanglement Scaling
summary: Local-operator entanglement (LOE) quantifies the nonlocal structure of Heisenberg operators and serves as a diagnostic of many-body chaos. We provide rigorous bounds showing when an operator can be well-approximated by a matrix-product operator (MPO), given asymptotic scaling of its LOE $α$-Rényi entropies. Specifically, we prove that a volume law scaling for $α\geq 1$ implies that the operator cannot be approximated efficiently as an MPO while faithfully reproducing all expectation values. On the other hand, if we restrict to correlations over a relevant sub-class of (ensembles of) states, then logarithmic scaling of the $α< 1$ Rényi LOE entropies implies MPO simulability. This result covers a range of relevant quantities, including infinite temperature autocorrelation functions, out-of-time-ordered correlators, and average-case expectation values over ensembles of computational basis states. Beyond this regime, we provide numerical evidence together with a random matrix model to argue that, also for out-of-equilibrium expectation values, logarithmic scaling for $α< 1$ Rényi LOE typically guarantees simulability. Our results put on firm footing the heuristic expectation that a low operator entanglement implies efficient tensor network representability, extending celebrated foundational results from the theory of matrix-product states and providing a formal link between quantum chaos and classical simulability.

AI.tldr: Rigorous bounds show when quantum operators can be approximated by matrix-product operators (MPOs) based on their local-operator entanglement (LOE) scaling: volume law for α≥1 prevents efficient MPO approximation, while logarithmic scaling for α<1 enables MPO simulability for relevant state ensembles.
AI.motivation: To establish formal connections between operator entanglement scaling, tensor network representability, and quantum chaos, providing rigorous foundations for the heuristic that low operator entanglement enables efficient classical simulation.
AI.method: Mathematical proofs of bounds relating LOE scaling to MPO approximability, numerical evidence, and random matrix modeling to analyze out-of-equilibrium expectation values.
AI.result: Volume law LOE scaling for α≥1 prevents efficient MPO approximation, while logarithmic scaling for α<1 enables MPO simulability for infinite temperature autocorrelations, OTOCs, and computational basis state ensembles.
AI.conclusion: The work provides rigorous foundations linking operator entanglement scaling to tensor network representability, formally connecting quantum chaos to classical simulability through LOE diagnostics.

title: Matchgate circuit representation of fermionic Gaussian states: optimal preparation, approximation, and classical simulation
summary: Fermionic Gaussian states (FGSs) and the associated matchgate circuits play a central role in quantum information theory and condensed matter physics. Despite being possibly highly entangled, they can still be efficiently simulated on classical computers. We address the question of how to optimally create such states when using matchgate circuits acting on product states. To this end, we derive lower bounds on the number of gates required to prepare an arbitrary pure FGS: We establish both an asymptotic bound on the minimal gate count over general nearest-neighbor gate sets and an exact bound for circuits composed solely of matchgates. We present explicit algorithms whose constructions saturate these bounds, thereby proving their optimality. We furthermore determine when an FGS can be prepared with a circuit of any given depth, and derive an algorithm that constructs such a circuit whenever this condition is satisfied, either exactly or approximately. Our results have direct applications to (approximate) state preparation and to disentangling procedures. Moreover, we introduce a new classical simulation algorithm for matchgate circuits, based entirely on manipulating the generating circuits of the FGSs. Finally, we briefly study an extension of our framework for $t$-doped Gaussian states and circuits.

AI.tldr: Optimal matchgate circuit construction for preparing fermionic Gaussian states with explicit algorithms saturating lower bounds on gate count and depth.
AI.motivation: Fermionic Gaussian states (FGSs) and matchgate circuits are important in quantum information and condensed matter physics. While classically simulable, the question of how to optimally create such states using matchgate circuits from product states remains open.
AI.method: Derived lower bounds on gate count for arbitrary pure FGS preparation: asymptotic bounds for general nearest-neighbor gate sets and exact bounds for pure matchgate circuits. Developed explicit algorithms that saturate these bounds, proving optimality. Also determined conditions for FGS preparation with given circuit depth and constructed corresponding circuits.
AI.result: Presented optimal algorithms for FGS preparation that achieve derived lower bounds. Introduced new classical simulation algorithm for matchgate circuits based on manipulating generating circuits of FGSs. Extended framework to t-doped Gaussian states and circuits.
AI.conclusion: The work provides complete characterization of optimal matchgate circuit construction for FGS preparation, with direct applications to state preparation, disentangling procedures, and classical simulation of matchgate circuits.

title: Order Unit Spaces and Probabilistic Models
summary: We exhibit a functor from the category OUS of order unit spaces and positive, unit-preserving mappings into the category $\Prob$ of probabilistic models (test spaces with designated state spaces) and morphisms thereof. Restricted to any subcategory of OUS monoidal with respect to a positive, normalized, bilinear composition rule, our functor is also monoidal. This shows that the convex-operational approach to physical theories can be subsumed by the test-space approach, without resort to ``generalized test spaces''. A second construction, equipping a probabilistic model with tests representing ``weighted coins'', also sheds light on the nature of unsharp observables.

AI.tldr: A functor maps order unit spaces to probabilistic models, showing convex-operational theories can be subsumed by test-space approach without generalized test spaces.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that the convex-operational approach to physical theories can be fully captured within the test-space framework without needing to resort to generalized test spaces, and to provide insights into the nature of unsharp observables.
AI.method: Construct a functor from the category of order unit spaces (OUS) to the category of probabilistic models (test spaces with state spaces). Show this functor is monoidal when restricted to subcategories of OUS with positive, normalized, bilinear composition rules. Provide a second construction that equips probabilistic models with tests representing "weighted coins".
AI.result: Successfully exhibits a functorial mapping that subsumes convex-operational theories within the test-space approach. The monoidal property holds for appropriate subcategories. The second construction provides insight into unsharp observables through weighted coin representations.
AI.conclusion: The convex-operational framework for physical theories can be fully embedded within the test-space approach without requiring generalized test spaces. The constructions also illuminate the mathematical nature of unsharp observables in quantum theory.

title: Steady-State Multiparticle Entanglement via Dissipative Engineering in Waveguide QED
summary: We propose a simple scheme for the dissipative generation of entangled states of multiple emitters coupled to a waveguide. Our approach exploits collective interactions arising from the formation of subradiant and superradiant excited states, combined with the quantum Zeno effect. We show that, starting from an arbitrary initial state, the system deterministically evolves toward a W-type entangled steady state, with an infidelity that scales inversely with the cooperativity. The protocol is scalable to an arbitrary number of emitters. We further analyze the impact of additional experimental imperfections and present a detailed implementation based on trapped $^{133}$Cs atoms.

AI.tldr: Dissipative generation of W-type entangled states for multiple emitters in a waveguide using collective interactions and quantum Zeno effect, with deterministic evolution and scalability.
AI.motivation: To develop a scalable method for generating entangled states of multiple quantum emitters in waveguide systems, addressing the challenge of deterministic entanglement generation in dissipative quantum systems.
AI.method: Exploits collective interactions from subradiant/superradiant excited states combined with quantum Zeno effect. Uses waveguide-coupled emitters where dissipation drives the system toward entangled steady states.
AI.result: System deterministically evolves from arbitrary initial state to W-type entangled steady state with infidelity scaling inversely with cooperativity. Protocol is scalable to arbitrary number of emitters.
AI.conclusion: Proposed scheme enables robust, scalable dissipative entanglement generation with implementation feasibility demonstrated using trapped Cs atoms, showing resilience to experimental imperfections.

title: Variational Quantum Eigensolver for the Analysis of High-Resolution NMR Spectra: Applications to AB and AB2 Spin Systems
summary: The Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are hybrid quantum-classical algorithms and they can be used in the Nosiy Intermadiate Scale Quantum (NISQ) devises. The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) was suggested as a first VQA. VQE is based on the variational method of quantum mechanics and it is used to find the ground state energy of a quantum system. In this study, VQE is used for the analysis of NMR spectra for the AB and AB2 spin systems. The frequencies and the spin coupling values are obtained from the sample spectra for these spin systems. Then the Hamiltonians are written in terms of pauli spin operators and transformed into a suitable forms for quantum computer. By employing VQE the ground state energies are obtained for the related spin systems. They are found to be in good agreement with the results obtained from the known variation method.

AI.tldr: VQE is applied to analyze NMR spectra of AB and AB2 spin systems, obtaining frequencies and coupling constants that match classical variational method results.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate the application of Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) for analyzing NMR spectra in NISQ devices, specifically for AB and AB2 spin systems, as a practical use case for quantum computing in spectroscopy.
AI.method: Extract frequencies and spin coupling values from NMR spectra of AB and AB2 spin systems, write Hamiltonians in terms of Pauli spin operators, transform them for quantum computation, then apply VQE to find ground state energies.
AI.result: Ground state energies obtained via VQE show good agreement with results from the classical variational method, validating VQE's applicability to NMR spectral analysis.
AI.conclusion: VQE can successfully analyze NMR spectra for simple spin systems, demonstrating the potential of variational quantum algorithms for spectroscopic applications on NISQ devices.

title: An Optimization Framework for Monitor Placement in Quantum Network Tomography
summary: Quantum Network Tomography (QNT) offers a framework for end-to-end quantum channel characterization by strategically placing monitor nodes within the network. Building upon prior work on single-monitor placement, we study optimal monitor placement and measurement assignments for channel parameter estimation in arbitrary quantum networks. Using an n-node star network as a baseline, we analyze multi-monitor configurations and show that distributing monitors across end nodes can achieve estimation performance comparable to a monitor placed at the hub. Estimation precision is quantified using the Quantum Fisher Information Matrix (QFIM), with channel parameters inferred via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and benchmarked against the Quantum Cramer-Rao Bound (QCRB). To generalize, we develop two Integer Linear Program (ILP) formulations: one maximizing estimation accuracy (QF), and another jointly optimizing accuracy and monitoring overhead (QMF). Unlike QF, QMF prevents monitor overloading, enabling scalability and parallelism. We prove optimality for star and analyze applicability to tree-structured quantum networks.

AI.tldr: Optimal monitor placement strategies for quantum network tomography using ILP formulations to balance estimation accuracy and monitoring overhead in arbitrary quantum networks.
AI.motivation: Extend single-monitor quantum network tomography to multi-monitor configurations for end-to-end quantum channel characterization in arbitrary quantum networks, addressing scalability and practical deployment challenges.
AI.method: Develop two Integer Linear Program (ILP) formulations: QF maximizes estimation accuracy using Quantum Fisher Information Matrix; QMF jointly optimizes accuracy and monitoring overhead to prevent monitor overloading. Analysis uses n-node star networks as baseline, with channel parameters inferred via Maximum Likelihood Estimation.
AI.result: Distributing monitors across end nodes achieves comparable estimation performance to hub placement; QMF formulation enables scalability and parallelism by preventing monitor overloading; optimality proven for star networks with applicability to tree-structured networks.
AI.conclusion: Multi-monitor configurations with optimized placement and measurement assignments provide practical quantum network tomography solutions, with ILP-based formulations offering scalable approaches for arbitrary quantum network topologies.

title: Rovibrational energy levels of H$_2$O by quantum computing
summary: We calculate rovibrational energy levels of H$_2$O using a trapped-ion quantum computer. We first derive the qubit form of Watson's Hamiltonian, including the rovibrational coupling terms. In a second step, we employ a variant of the quantum-selected configuration-interaction method to calculate rovibrational energy levels. A truncated form of the qubit Hamiltonian is used to generate correlated rovibrational wave functions on the quantum computer by time evolution, and a basis set is selected by sampling from the measured probability distribution. The rovibrational energy levels are obtained by constructing a Hamiltonian matrix using the selected basis set, and diagonalizing the matrix using a classical computer. We show that an accuracy of a few cm$^{-1}$ can be achieved for low-lying rovibrational energy levels.

AI.tldr: Quantum computing approach calculates H2O rovibrational energy levels using trapped-ion quantum computer with quantum-selected configuration-interaction method, achieving few cm⁻¹ accuracy for low-lying states.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate quantum computing applications in molecular spectroscopy by calculating accurate rovibrational energy levels of water molecules using quantum hardware.
AI.method: Derived qubit form of Watson's Hamiltonian including rovibrational coupling terms, used quantum-selected configuration-interaction method with truncated Hamiltonian for time evolution on trapped-ion quantum computer, sampled probability distribution to select basis set, constructed Hamiltonian matrix classically and diagonalized it.
AI.result: Achieved accuracy of a few cm⁻¹ for low-lying rovibrational energy levels of H2O using the quantum computing approach.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computers can be effectively used for molecular spectroscopy calculations, specifically for rovibrational energy level determination, with promising accuracy for low-lying states.

title: Robust coherent control in non-Hermitian cavity electromagnonics using counterdiabatic driving
summary: We propose to use counterdiabatic driving (CD) shortcut and the Floquet engineering to realize the robust and fast state transfer in the dissipation cavity magnon-polaritons non-Hermitian (NH) system. For the two-level NH cavity magnon-polaritons Hamiltonian, an accurate and fast population transfer is achieved from the microwave photon to the magnon by two coherent control techniques; counterdiabatic driving shortcut and non-Hermitian shortcuts (NHSs). Additionally, by using the CD technique, the population evolution speed of non-Hermitian systems is faster than that via the NHS technique in the broken-symmetric regime. Furthermore, we compare their performances in the presence of the coupling strength and systematic errors, the CD technique features a broad range of high efficiencies of the transition probability above 99.9%, showing that the CD technique is more robustness against these errors than the NHS technique. It is worth noting that this advantage becomes more significant as the gain rate of system parameters increases. The work provides a basis for achieving the robust coherent control in NH cavity electromagnonics.

AI.tldr: Counterdiabatic driving and Floquet engineering enable robust, fast state transfer in non-Hermitian cavity magnon-polaritons systems, with CD outperforming non-Hermitian shortcuts in speed and error tolerance.
AI.motivation: To achieve robust and fast state transfer in dissipation cavity magnon-polaritons non-Hermitian systems, addressing the need for efficient coherent control techniques in non-Hermitian quantum systems.
AI.method: Combines counterdiabatic driving shortcut and Floquet engineering with non-Hermitian shortcuts for two-level NH cavity magnon-polaritons Hamiltonian; compares CD and NHS techniques for population transfer from microwave photons to magnons.
AI.result: CD achieves faster population evolution than NHS in broken-symmetric regime; CD maintains >99.9% transition probability across broad parameter ranges and shows superior robustness against coupling strength and systematic errors, especially with higher gain rates.
AI.conclusion: Counterdiabatic driving provides a superior approach for robust coherent control in non-Hermitian cavity electromagnonics, offering faster, more error-tolerant state transfer compared to non-Hermitian shortcuts.

title: Gaussian dynamics in the double Siegel disk
summary: We show that multimode deterministic (CPTP) Gaussian channels admit a symmetric-space description: by passing from the \(n\)-mode Siegel disk \(Δ_{n}\) to the \(2n\)-mode \emph{double Siegel disk} \(Δ_{2n}\), general Gaussian dynamics becomes a linear-fractional (Möbius) action on a single matrix representative. Concretely, \(Δ_{2n}\) naturally parametrizes Gaussian kernels in the Fock--Bargmann representation, and we identify an explicit physical subset \(\sspace\subsetΔ_{2n}\) corresponding to valid mixed Gaussian states. We then construct, from the standard \((X,Y)\) parametrization of a deterministic Gaussian channel, a normalized oscillator-semigroup element \(\bar E\) whose fractional action implements the channel update \(\amat\mapstoφ_{\bar E}(\amat)\) on \(\sspace\); Gaussian unitaries arise as the symplectic (isometric) subcase. The resulting calculus bridges covariance-matrix channel theory with the adjacency-matrix/symmetric-space picture, retains a simple composition law (matrix multiplication of the acting blocks), and suggests a direct route to graphical update rules beyond the pure-state setting.

AI.tldr: Gaussian channels have symmetric-space representation via double Siegel disk, enabling linear-fractional action on Gaussian states with simple composition rules.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified mathematical framework for describing multimode deterministic Gaussian channels that bridges covariance-matrix theory with symmetric-space geometry, providing simpler composition laws and enabling extensions beyond pure-state settings.
AI.method: Extend from n-mode Siegel disk to 2n-mode double Siegel disk, identify physical subset corresponding to valid mixed Gaussian states, construct normalized oscillator-semigroup elements whose fractional action implements channel updates, with Gaussian unitaries as symplectic subcase.
AI.result: Established symmetric-space description of Gaussian channels with linear-fractional (Möbius) action on matrix representatives, simple composition via matrix multiplication, and connection between covariance-matrix theory and symmetric-space picture.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a unified calculus for Gaussian channels with elegant mathematical structure, enabling graphical update rules and extending beyond pure-state settings while maintaining physical interpretability.

title: Variational Quantum Algorithm for Constrained Combinatorial Optimization Problems
summary: While variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) have demonstrated considerable success in unconstrained optimization, their application to constrained combinatorial problems face a trade-off. Penalty-based methods, despite their circuit simplicity, suffer from a fundamental limitation: inefficient sampling in vast infeasible regions. This often results in suboptimal solutions that violate constraints and impede convergence to high-quality results. In contrast, ansatz-based approaches enforce solution feasibility by design but require complex, problem-specific circuits that are challenging to implement on current noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. To overcome these limitations, we introduce an alternative VQA whose core innovation lies in a strategically designed loss function. This function offers a dual advantage. First, it is provably guaranteed that its global minimum corresponds uniquely to the optimal feasible solution, as this is achieved by ensuring universally higher loss values for all infeasible solutions. Second, it furnishes distinct computational pathways for feasible versus infeasible regions, thus creating clear and non competing guidance for the optimizer. As a result of these combined features, the algorithm's overall performance is significantly enhanced. Regarding hardware overhead, our design requires adding only an efficient validation oracle module to the penalty-based circuit, resulting in a circuit complexity significantly lower than that of ansatz-based approaches with their custom mixers. To validate the practical efficiency of our method, we empirically demonstrate its effectiveness by solving minimum vertex cover and maximum independent set problems on random graphs of varying small-scale sizes.

AI.tldr: A novel variational quantum algorithm with a strategically designed loss function that guarantees global minimum corresponds uniquely to optimal feasible solution, overcoming limitations of penalty-based and ansatz-based approaches for constrained combinatorial optimization.
AI.motivation: Current VQAs for constrained combinatorial problems face a trade-off: penalty-based methods suffer from inefficient sampling in infeasible regions, while ansatz-based approaches require complex, problem-specific circuits that are challenging to implement on NISQ devices.
AI.method: Introduces a VQA with a strategically designed loss function that: 1) guarantees global minimum uniquely corresponds to optimal feasible solution by ensuring universally higher loss values for all infeasible solutions, 2) provides distinct computational pathways for feasible vs infeasible regions, creating clear guidance for optimizer. Requires adding only an efficient validation oracle module to penalty-based circuits.
AI.result: Empirical validation on minimum vertex cover and maximum independent set problems on random graphs of varying small-scale sizes demonstrates practical efficiency. Circuit complexity is significantly lower than ansatz-based approaches with custom mixers.
AI.conclusion: The proposed VQA overcomes limitations of existing approaches by combining theoretical guarantees (global minimum corresponds to optimal feasible solution) with practical advantages (lower circuit complexity, clear optimization guidance), making it suitable for constrained combinatorial optimization on NISQ devices.

title: Heterogeneous entanglement between a trapped ion and a solid-state quantum memory
summary: Hybrid quantum networks offer a promising architecture for scalable quantum information processing and a future quantum internet, as they can combine the complementary strengths of disparate physical platforms. While single-atom systems provide deterministic quantum logic gates, atomic ensembles enable large-capacity quantum storage. However, generating entanglement between such heterogeneous systems has remained an open challenge, primarily due to fundamental spectral mismatches and system complexity. Here, we demonstrate a hybrid quantum network that entangles a single trapped $\mathrm{^{171}Yb^{+}}$ ion and a quantum memory based on $\rm ^{153}Eu^{3+}\colon\!Y_2SiO_5$ crystal over a 75-m separation. Using polarization-maintaining quantum frequency conversion, we map spin-photon entanglement onto a hybrid entanglement between a single spin qubit and a collective excitation of the quantum memory. The resulting entangled state achieves a fidelity of $(89.21 \pm 2.23)\%$ and violates the CHSH-Bell inequality by 6 standard deviations ($S = 2.328 \pm 0.055$), confirming nonlocality between two heterogeneous nodes. This work establishes entanglement between a quantum processing module with a multiplexed quantum memory node, representing a key step toward a scalable, multifunctional quantum internet.

AI.tldr: Demonstration of hybrid quantum network entangling a single trapped Yb+ ion qubit with a Eu:Y2SiO5 crystal quantum memory over 75m using quantum frequency conversion, achieving 89.21% fidelity and Bell inequality violation.
AI.motivation: Hybrid quantum networks combine complementary strengths of different physical platforms for scalable quantum information processing, but entanglement between heterogeneous systems has been challenging due to spectral mismatches and complexity.
AI.method: Used polarization-maintaining quantum frequency conversion to map spin-photon entanglement onto hybrid entanglement between a single spin qubit (trapped Yb+ ion) and collective excitation of a quantum memory (Eu:Y2SiO5 crystal), connecting nodes over 75m separation.
AI.result: Achieved entangled state fidelity of (89.21 ± 2.23)% and violated CHSH-Bell inequality by 6 standard deviations (S = 2.328 ± 0.055), confirming nonlocality between heterogeneous quantum nodes.
AI.conclusion: Established entanglement between quantum processing module and multiplexed quantum memory node, representing key step toward scalable, multifunctional quantum internet architecture.

title: Casimir-Polder potential on an excited atom near an atomic array
summary: We develop a microscopic description of the fluctuation-mediated Casimir-Polder (CP) shifts on a 'test' two-level atom placed near a two-dimensional atomic array of two-level atoms. We derive the resonant and off-resonant CP potentials experienced by the excited test atom using fourth-order perturbation theory, under the assumption that the test atom resonance is far detuned from those of the array atoms. The total potential on the test atom can be described as the sum of the pairwise resonant and off-resonant potentials resulting from its interaction with the individual atoms of the array. We analyze the asymptotic scaling of CP shifts as a function of the test atom-array separation, and its dependence on various system parameters: array spacing and size, and dipole orientation of the array atoms. Our results bridge the description of CP potential across two distinct regimes: (i) from a single-atom limit where we recover the well-known two-atom Van der Waals potential, (ii) to a macroscopic boundary limit, where we demonstrate new asymptotic scaling laws. We demonstrate that these scaling laws can be tuned via the microscopic parameters of the atomic array, establishing atomically-controlled arrays as a versatile platform for tailoring fluctuation-induced QED phenomena.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a microscopic theory for Casimir-Polder shifts on a test atom near a 2D atomic array, deriving resonant and off-resonant potentials using fourth-order perturbation theory and analyzing asymptotic scaling laws.
AI.motivation: To provide a microscopic description of fluctuation-mediated Casimir-Polder shifts on a test atom near a two-dimensional atomic array, bridging the gap between single-atom Van der Waals potentials and macroscopic boundary effects.
AI.method: Fourth-order perturbation theory is used to derive resonant and off-resonant Casimir-Polder potentials, assuming the test atom resonance is far detuned from array atoms. The total potential is expressed as sum of pairwise interactions with individual array atoms.
AI.result: The theory recovers two-atom Van der Waals potential in single-atom limit and demonstrates new asymptotic scaling laws in macroscopic boundary limit. Scaling laws can be tuned via microscopic parameters (array spacing, size, dipole orientation).
AI.conclusion: Atomic arrays serve as a versatile platform for tailoring fluctuation-induced QED phenomena, with tunable Casimir-Polder potentials bridging microscopic and macroscopic regimes.

title: Multi-Shot Quantum Sensing for RF Signal Detection with MIMO Rydberg-Atom Receivers
comment: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC 2026), Kobe, Japan
summary: Rydberg-atom quantum receivers (RAQRs) enable electric-field sensing with quantum-noise-limited performance, yet their optical readout provides only magnitude measurements whose fluctuations follow Rician statistics governed by atomic projection noise, optical shot noise, reference-field injection, and short coherence times. These non-Gaussian, phase-blind measurements invalidate classical single-shot RF detectors and necessitate multi-shot quantum sensing strategies. This work develops a physically consistent multi-shot statistical model for RAQRs and derives both the optimal genie-aided likelihood-ratio test (LRT) and a practical phase-averaged LRT that removes dependence on the unknown RF-field phase. Closed-form test statistics and thresholds are obtained for both detectors, and the limits imposed by finite quantum shots-due to atomic dephasing and measurement backaction-are explicitly quantified. A fully non-coherent energy detector is also analysed, with exact detection probability derived using noncentral chi-square models. Monte Carlo results show that only 5-10 quantum shots yield major gains: the phase-averaged LRT closely approaches the genie bound and RAQR detection markedly outperforms classical RF energy detection under comparable received power. The proposed framework provides the first unified statistical basis for multi-shot Rydberg-based weak-field detection and underscores the potential of RAQRs for quantum-enhanced signal detection.

AI.tldr: Develops statistical models for multi-shot Rydberg-atom quantum receivers, deriving optimal and practical likelihood-ratio tests for weak RF field detection with quantum-enhanced performance.
AI.motivation: Rydberg-atom quantum receivers provide quantum-noise-limited electric-field sensing but produce non-Gaussian, phase-blind measurements that invalidate classical single-shot RF detectors, necessitating multi-shot quantum sensing strategies.
AI.method: Develops physically consistent multi-shot statistical model for RAQRs, derives optimal genie-aided likelihood-ratio test and practical phase-averaged LRT, analyzes fully non-coherent energy detector using noncentral chi-square models, and quantifies limits from finite quantum shots.
AI.result: Only 5-10 quantum shots yield major gains: phase-averaged LRT closely approaches genie bound, and RAQR detection markedly outperforms classical RF energy detection under comparable received power.
AI.conclusion: Provides first unified statistical basis for multi-shot Rydberg-based weak-field detection and underscores potential of RAQRs for quantum-enhanced signal detection.

title: Classical simulability of quantum circuits followed by sparse classical post-processing
summary: We study the classical simulability of a polynomial-size quantum circuit $C_n$ on $n$ qubits followed by sparse classical post-processing (SCP) on $m$ bits, where $m \leq n \leq {\rm poly}(m)$. The SCP is described by a non-zero Boolean function $f_m$ that is classically computable in polynomial time and is sparse, i.e., has a peaked Fourier spectrum. First, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition on $C_n$ such that, for any SCP $f_m$, $C_n$ followed by $f_m$ is classically simulable. This characterization extends the result of Van den Nest and implies that various quantum circuits followed by SCP are classically simulable. Examples include IQP circuits, Clifford Magic circuits, and the quantum part of Simon's algorithm, even though these circuits alone are hard to simulate classically. Then, we consider the case where $C_n$ has constant depth $d$. While it is unlikely that, for any SCP $f_m$, $C_n$ followed by $f_m$ is classically simulable, we show that it is simulable by a polynomial-time probabilistic algorithm with access to commuting quantum circuits on $n+1$ qubits. Each such circuit consists of at most deg($f_m$) commuting gates and each commuting gate acts on at most $2^d+1$ qubits, where deg($f_m$) is the Fourier degree of $f_m$. This provides a better understanding of the hardness of simulating constant-depth quantum circuits followed by SCP.

AI.tldr: The paper studies classical simulability of polynomial-size quantum circuits followed by sparse classical post-processing, providing characterization theorems and simulation algorithms.
AI.motivation: To understand when quantum circuits with classical post-processing become classically simulable, particularly focusing on circuits that are hard to simulate alone but become tractable when combined with sparse classical processing.
AI.method: Provides necessary and sufficient conditions for classical simulability of quantum circuits with sparse classical post-processing, extends Van den Nest's result, and develops polynomial-time probabilistic algorithms with access to commuting quantum circuits for constant-depth cases.
AI.result: Shows that various quantum circuits (IQP, Clifford Magic, Simon's algorithm quantum part) become classically simulable when followed by sparse classical post-processing, and provides efficient simulation algorithms for constant-depth circuits using commuting quantum circuits.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive characterization of classical simulability for quantum circuits with sparse classical post-processing, revealing that many quantum circuits that are hard to simulate alone become tractable when combined with appropriate classical processing, advancing understanding of quantum-classical computational boundaries.

title: Significant modifications of Lamb shift at small centripetal accelerations
summary: We investigate the Lamb shift of centripetally accelerated atoms coupled to electromagnetic vacuum fluctuations. Focusing on a very small orbital radius (so that the tangential speed remains nonrelativistic and the proper centripetal acceleration can be extremely small), we show that the resulting level shift is intrinsically anisotropic and depends sensitively on the atomic polarization direction. For atoms polarizable along the rotation axis, the leading noninertial contribution enters only at second order in the orbital radius and can slightly decrease or increase the energy-level spacing, depending on the angular-velocity regime. In contrast, for atoms polarizable perpendicular to the rotation axis, the noninertial contribution appears already at the leading order in the radius and always increases the energy-level spacing. Remarkably, when the angular velocity greatly exceeds the transition frequency, the rotation-induced correction can become comparable in magnitude to the inertial Lamb shift, indicating that circular motion can significantly modify the Lamb shift even in the regime of very small centripetal accelerations.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how circular motion affects the Lamb shift of atoms in vacuum, showing that even with small centripetal acceleration, rotation induces anisotropic corrections that can be comparable to inertial Lamb shifts.
AI.motivation: To understand how non-inertial motion, specifically circular acceleration, modifies quantum electrodynamic effects like the Lamb shift, which has implications for atomic physics in rotating systems and tests of quantum field theory in non-inertial frames.
AI.method: Analyze centripetally accelerated atoms coupled to electromagnetic vacuum fluctuations, focusing on small orbital radii where tangential speed is nonrelativistic but proper centripetal acceleration can be extremely small. Calculate Lamb shift contributions for different atomic polarization directions relative to rotation axis.
AI.result: The Lamb shift becomes intrinsically anisotropic and polarization-dependent. For axial polarization, non-inertial contributions appear at second order in orbital radius and can either decrease or increase energy spacing depending on angular velocity. For perpendicular polarization, corrections appear at leading order and always increase energy spacing. When angular velocity greatly exceeds transition frequency, rotation-induced corrections can become comparable to inertial Lamb shift.
AI.conclusion: Circular motion can significantly modify the Lamb shift even with very small centripetal accelerations, revealing anisotropic, polarization-dependent effects that challenge the notion that only acceleration magnitude matters, suggesting rotation itself has distinct quantum electrodynamic consequences.

title: Characterizing Noise Effects on Multipartite Entanglement via Phase-Space Visualization
summary: This paper investigates the behavior of two fundamental types of multipartite entangled states, namely GHZ(3) and W(3) states under Gaussian-distributed amplitude perturbations and White noise model. The Uhlmann-Jozsa fidelity is taken to be the quantitative measure to show the overall degradation of the quantum states, and is implemented via TQIX : a tool specifically designed for quantum state measurement and related applications. While fidelity analysis captures the progressive decay of quantum states under noise, it offers only limited understanding regarding the state decay and doesn't provide a detailed analysis of how entanglement structures respond to noise models. To reveal the phase-space characteristics and nonclassical signatures of three-qubit entangled states, we employ the spin Wigner function using equal-angle projection. This approach reveals a continuous fading of quantum coherence with increasing noise strength, ultimately providing a clear picture of transition toward classical-like behavior in phase space. This combined qualitative-quantitative framework provides deeper understanding of how different entanglement structures respond to noise, offering practical applications for designing and implementing noise resilient protocols in quantum computing, and quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: Analysis of GHZ(3) and W(3) states under Gaussian amplitude perturbations and white noise using fidelity measures and spin Wigner functions to understand entanglement degradation and phase-space behavior.
AI.motivation: To understand how different multipartite entanglement structures (GHZ and W states) degrade under noise models, and to move beyond simple fidelity measures to reveal detailed phase-space characteristics and entanglement responses to noise.
AI.method: Used Uhlmann-Jozsa fidelity via TQIX tool for quantitative state degradation measurement, combined with spin Wigner function using equal-angle projection to reveal phase-space characteristics and nonclassical signatures of three-qubit entangled states under Gaussian-distributed amplitude perturbations and white noise.
AI.result: Fidelity analysis shows progressive decay of quantum states under noise, while spin Wigner functions reveal continuous fading of quantum coherence with increasing noise strength, showing transition toward classical-like behavior in phase space. The combined approach provides deeper understanding of how different entanglement structures respond to noise.
AI.conclusion: The qualitative-quantitative framework combining fidelity measures with phase-space analysis offers practical applications for designing noise-resilient protocols in quantum computing and quantum information processing by providing detailed understanding of entanglement degradation mechanisms.

title: Variational Quantum Operator Simulation
summary: Implementing time-evolution operators in shallow quantum circuits is important for quantum simulations. The standard method of Trotterization requires a large number of gates to achieve practical accuracy. Variational Quantum Simulation (VQS) is an algorithm that calculates the time evolution of a quantum state and can be executed with shallower circuits than Trotterization. However, the operator obtained by VQS evolves only a fixed initial state and is not the time evolution operator itself. In this paper, we propose Variational Quantum Operator Simulation (VQOS), a method to realize time evolution operators in shallow quantum circuits. This method is based on the variational principle for operators and does not require the implementation of the desired Trotter decomposition of the time evolution operator. We performed numerical simulations of the VQOS algorithm and successfully implemented the time evolution operator for closed systems in a quantum circuit that is up to 5 times shallower than the Trotterization. By providing a more practical way to implement time evolution operators, VQOS increases the applicability of near-term quantum computers.

AI.tldr: VQOS (Variational Quantum Operator Simulation) enables implementation of time evolution operators in shallower quantum circuits than Trotterization, increasing near-term quantum computer applicability.
AI.motivation: Standard Trotterization requires many gates for practical accuracy, while existing Variational Quantum Simulation (VQS) only evolves fixed initial states rather than implementing the time evolution operator itself.
AI.method: VQOS uses variational principle for operators to realize time evolution operators in shallow quantum circuits without requiring Trotter decomposition implementation.
AI.result: Numerical simulations show VQOS successfully implements time evolution operators for closed systems in circuits up to 5 times shallower than Trotterization.
AI.conclusion: VQOS provides a more practical way to implement time evolution operators, increasing the applicability of near-term quantum computers for quantum simulations.

title: Grand Canonical-like Thermalization of Quantum Many-body Scars
summary: Quantum many-body scar (QMBS) in kinetically constrained quantum systems challenges the conventional eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH). We develop an effective open-system description for constrained dynamics and introduce the definition of quasiparticle number in the system. Based on this, we formulate a revised ETH that accounts for both diagonal and off-diagonal structures of local observables. By introducing the cross coherence purity (CCP), we obtain a unified characterization of off-diagonal matrix elements and show that the relevant density of states (DOS) is determined by the distribution of eigenstates on the energy--quasiparticle-number plane. We numerically verify an inverse relation between the CCP and this generalized DOS. Applied to the quantum many-body scar model, the revised ETH accurately predicts long-time averages and temporal fluctuations of local observables and explains their dependence on initial states. Our framework shows that the anomalous fluctuations and quasi-periodic dynamics of scar states arise naturally from low-DOS regions. These results provide a unified understanding of thermalization and QMBS in kinetically constrained systems.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a revised eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) framework for kinetically constrained quantum systems, explaining quantum many-body scars through low density of states regions and predicting local observable dynamics.
AI.motivation: Quantum many-body scars challenge conventional ETH in constrained systems, requiring a theoretical framework that can explain both thermalization and anomalous scar dynamics.
AI.method: Develop effective open-system description for constrained dynamics, define quasiparticle number, formulate revised ETH accounting for diagonal/off-diagonal structures, introduce cross coherence purity (CCP), analyze density of states distribution on energy-quasiparticle-number plane.
AI.result: Numerical verification of inverse relation between CCP and generalized DOS; revised ETH accurately predicts long-time averages and temporal fluctuations of local observables; explains scar state anomalous fluctuations and quasi-periodic dynamics from low-DOS regions.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides unified understanding of thermalization and quantum many-body scars in kinetically constrained systems, showing scar anomalies arise naturally from low density of states regions.

title: Macroscopic entanglement distribution with atomic ensembles
summary: The distribution of entanglement is a crucial task for quantum communication towards realizing a globe-spanning quantum internet. Recently a protocol for deterministic long-distance distribution of macroscopic entanglement over a network of ensembles of qubits was introduced [Adv. Quantum Technol. 2025, 8, 2400524]. It was shown that this protocol allows for the propagation of macroscopic amounts of entanglement with a protocol complexity that is independent on the ensemble size. However, questions remained on whether the scheme is viable, particularly for a large particle number, which is the case for realistic atomic ensembles. Here we develop improved numerical techniques that allow calculation of realistic ensemble sizes up to 10^6 with a negligible loss of accuracy. We find that moderate dephasing leaves the entanglement largely intact at the magic times, whereas stronger noise monotonically suppresses the entanglement. Our results demonstrate that the protocol retains its functionality towards the macroscopic regime and provides quantitative benchmarks for its robustness under a realistic level of decoherence.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that a protocol for deterministic long-distance distribution of macroscopic entanglement over qubit ensembles remains viable for realistic ensemble sizes up to 10^6 particles, showing robustness to moderate dephasing but suppression under stronger noise.
AI.motivation: To investigate the viability of a previously introduced protocol for deterministic long-distance distribution of macroscopic entanglement over qubit ensembles, particularly for large particle numbers relevant to realistic atomic ensembles, and to assess its robustness under realistic decoherence.
AI.method: Development of improved numerical techniques enabling calculation of realistic ensemble sizes up to 10^6 with negligible accuracy loss, used to analyze the protocol's performance under dephasing and noise conditions.
AI.result: The protocol retains functionality in the macroscopic regime; moderate dephasing leaves entanglement largely intact at magic times, while stronger noise monotonically suppresses entanglement. Quantitative benchmarks for robustness under realistic decoherence levels are provided.
AI.conclusion: The protocol for deterministic long-distance distribution of macroscopic entanglement remains viable for realistic ensemble sizes, demonstrating robustness to moderate decoherence and providing practical benchmarks for implementation.

title: Quantum chemistry based on classical mechanics inspired by simulated bifurcation
summary: Accurate quantum chemical calculations are critical for understanding molecular properties, yet their computational cost remains a major challenge. Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) provides exact solutions but is prohibitively expensive for large systems. To address this, quantum computers are expected to be useful, but developing practical quantum computers is still ongoing. Here we introduce an efficient Configuration Interaction (CI) computation algorithm based on classical mechanics, which we call Simulated Bifurcation-based CI (SBCI), because we derive this algorithm from a quantum inspired algorithm for combinatorial optimization called Simulated Bifurcation. Applying it to FCI computations of representative molecular systems and comparing the results with those by a standard method, we demonstrate that SBCI can reduce computation costs such as computation times and/or required memory sizes, while keeping high accuracy comparable to the standard method. Thus, SBCI will be promising for accelerating high-precision electronic structure calculations without compromising reliability.

AI.tldr: SBCI is a classical quantum-inspired algorithm that reduces computational costs for Full Configuration Interaction calculations while maintaining high accuracy comparable to standard methods.
AI.motivation: Full Configuration Interaction provides exact quantum chemical solutions but is computationally prohibitive for large systems. While quantum computers are promising for this problem, they are not yet practical, creating a need for efficient classical alternatives.
AI.method: Simulated Bifurcation-based CI (SBCI) adapts a quantum-inspired combinatorial optimization algorithm called Simulated Bifurcation to Configuration Interaction computations, creating an efficient classical algorithm for electronic structure calculations.
AI.result: SBCI significantly reduces computation times and memory requirements for FCI calculations on representative molecular systems while maintaining accuracy comparable to standard methods.
AI.conclusion: SBCI offers a promising approach for accelerating high-precision electronic structure calculations without compromising reliability, providing an efficient classical alternative while practical quantum computers are still under development.

title: Vertical ion transport in a surface Paul trap: escalator and elevator approaches
summary: Surface ion traps confining and manipulating tens of ion qubits have become the leading platform for quantum processors with high quantum volume. These devices employ the Quantum Charge-Coupled Device (QCCD) architecture, wherein multiple trapping zones are linked by an on-chip transport network that shuttles ion chains, enabling full connectivity through physical ion transport in a plane parallel to the chip surface. The ability to move ions perpendicular to this plane can offer additional advantages, including tuning the laser-ion interaction strength, systematic studies of surface-induced heating mechanisms, and precise alignment with a mode of an external optical cavity. We introduce an "escalator" - a geometrically optimized transition between trapping zones of different confinement heights - and present a comparative analysis of two "elevator" configurations that reposition the RF null dynamically via additional electrode voltages. Both approaches enable nearly a twofold change in the ion confinement height above the chip surface.

AI.tldr: Researchers introduce "escalator" and "elevator" configurations for surface ion traps to enable vertical ion movement, allowing nearly twofold changes in confinement height above the chip surface.
AI.motivation: While surface ion traps with QCCD architecture enable planar ion transport, vertical ion movement offers additional advantages: tuning laser-ion interaction strength, studying surface-induced heating mechanisms, and precise alignment with external optical cavities.
AI.method: Two approaches: 1) "Escalator" - geometrically optimized transition between trapping zones of different confinement heights; 2) "Elevator" configurations - reposition RF null dynamically via additional electrode voltages.
AI.result: Both approaches enable nearly a twofold change in ion confinement height above the chip surface, providing vertical positioning capability.
AI.conclusion: The introduced escalator and elevator configurations extend the capabilities of surface ion traps beyond planar transport, enabling vertical ion positioning for enhanced quantum processor functionality.

title: Summing to Uncertainty: On the Necessity of Additivity in Deriving the Born Rule
summary:
The emergence of intrinsic probability has long been one of the most important and puzzling problems in quantum mechanics, and the law most directly related to this problem is the Born rule. For a century, there have been many attempts to derive the Born rule as a theorem rather than postulating it. However, existing derivations of the Born rule are each based on different frameworks and have attracted different criticisms. The assumptions from which they start are also highly divergent, and the connections between them have not been sufficiently studied. These possible connections are very likely to be the key to answering questions about the origin of probability in quantum mechanics.
  This paper focuses on proving the necessity and indispensability of the additivity assumption in the derivation of the Born rule. This supports the view that the Born rule cannot be derived solely from other non-probabilistic quantum or additional postulates. We first prove that additivity cannot be derived from two other commonly used non-probabilistic additional assumptions, non-contextuality and normalization. Then we analyze the crucial role of the additivity assumption in five important existing derivations of the Born rule. These include Gleason's Theorem, Busch's extension of Gleason's Theorem, the Deutsch-Wallace Theorem, Zurek's envariance proof, and the Finkelstein-Hartle Theorem. We show that these derivations either depend heavily on the additivity assumption or lead to obvious loopholes due to the lack of additivity. We also point out some problems arised from the lack of a non-contextuality assumption.
  Our results provide a novel insight into the important role of additivity assumption in quantum measurement, as well as into the origin of probability in quantum mechanics.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the necessity of the additivity assumption in deriving the Born rule, showing it cannot be derived from non-contextuality and normalization alone, and examines its crucial role in five major Born rule derivations.
AI.motivation: To address the long-standing puzzle of intrinsic probability in quantum mechanics by investigating whether the Born rule can be derived without probabilistic postulates, specifically examining the indispensability of the additivity assumption in existing derivations.
